title: Ang 345–346: Begampura
hookLine: Ravidas's city without sorrow closes Gauri
tomorrow: why does Asa open with a hymn you may already know?

lines: A PERFECT CITY, IN A HYMN.
NO SORROW. NO FEAR. NO TAX?
cards: Every home listing sells the same dream: a quiet street, good schools, low taxes. On ang 345 there's a poem about a perfect city, and here's the odd part. Among the things it doesn't have, it lists taxes.
Not only sorrow and fear: taxes, property, a gate that keeps people out. Who puts a tax office into a hymn? The poet signs his name at the end.

teach.b: Ravidas tells you who he is in the hymn's last line, in paraphrase: says Ravidas, the leatherworker, now set free.

teach.h: NO SORROW, NO TAX, NO FEAR.
teach.b: His city is Begampura, the city without sorrow. Here it is, in paraphrase: no pain or worry lives there; no anxiety, no tax, no property to guard; no fear, no fault, no dread of falling.
There's no second or third rank there; all are one. People go wherever they please, and no one at the palace stops them. Now the puzzle solves itself.

Ravidas isn't listing what heaven lacks in general. He's listing what pressed on people like him: the tax collector, the fear, the rank you were born into, the door you weren't let through. His city has none of it.
Then he says, in paraphrase, now I have found this fine homeland, and it's well there, always, my brother. Readers differ on what Begampura is: a state of the soul, a city still to be built, or both.

teach.h: WHOEVER LIVES THERE IS MY FRIEND.
teach.b: It ends with an invitation instead: whoever is a citizen there is my friend.
A page later, Gauri closes, its last word given to a welcome.

how: Ravidas's Begampura hymn is read in order near the close of Raag Gauri and is also sung as kirtan; Sikhs and the followers of Ravidas both hold his hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib dear.

o: the page where Ravidas names the city without sorrow
the page where Guru Nanak's Asa hymns begin
the last page of the whole Guru Granth Sahib

games.q: the city without sorrow — tap the pairs.
p: signs as a leatherworker, set free

s: Begampura is just a pretty word for heaven, with nothing earthly in it
Ravidas lists very earthly things it lacks: tax, property, fear, rank, a gate that keeps people out.
Ravidas names himself as a leatherworker in the hymn
the last line: says Ravidas, the leatherworker, now set free.
readers agree Begampura is only a place after death
some read it as the soul's state, some as a city to build, some as both; the hymn doesn't settle it.

games.q: your club votes on a new rule: seniors get first pick of everything. you're a senior. what fits ang 345?
o: vote no: in Ravidas's city there's no second or third rank.
vote yes: you waited your turn, so the rank is earned.
skip the vote: a hymn about a city has nothing to say about clubs.
games.why: Begampura has no second or third rank and no one stopped at the palace door. Ravidas lists the very things that pressed people down.

practice: Read ang 345 slowly if you can. Then look at the nearest door, the front door or the one to this room, for the whole sit.
Let it stand for every door that's ever been shut on someone, and rest in Ravidas's picture of a city where it simply opens.
